8 Practice
These exercises emphasize interpretation and the choice of method. Numerical answers should be accompanied by a short explanation of what the computed quantity means. ::: practice-box 1. A surprise is relative to a model. Two analysts consider the same event. Analyst A assigns probability 0.20; Analyst B assigns probability 0.02. Calculate each analyst’s surprisal if the event occurs, in nats. Why is it incorrect to say that the event has a unique surprisal independent of the analysts? :::






NoteSuggested solution





The surprisals are

I_A=-\log(0.20)\approx 1.609\text{ nats},\qquad
I_B=-\log(0.02)\approx 3.912\text{ nats}.

Analyst B is more surprised because B assigned the event a lower probability. Surprisal is a function of an outcome and a probability assignment; the event alone does not determine it. Neither calculation tells us which analyst is better calibrated without additional observations or information about the process.




2. Expected surprise. Let X take the values a,b,c with probabilities (0.5,0.3,0.2). Calculate H(X) in nats. Identify which outcome has the greatest surprisal and explain why that does not imply it makes the largest contribution to entropy.







NoteSuggested solution





Using natural logarithms,

\begin{aligned}
H(X)&=-0.5\log(0.5)-0.3\log(0.3)-0.2\log(0.2)\\
&\approx 1.030\text{ nats}.
\end{aligned}

Outcome c has the largest individual surprisal, because it is the least probable:

I(a)\approx0.693,\qquad I(b)\approx1.204,\qquad I(c)\approx1.609.

But entropy averages surprisal over outcomes. The three contributions -p(x)\log p(x) are approximately 0.347, 0.361, and 0.322 nats. Outcome b contributes the most because it is sufficiently surprising and occurs more frequently than c. The most surprising outcome need not make the largest contribution to expected surprise.




3. Coarsening an outcome. A fair eight-sided die is rolled. First define X as the exact result; then define Y as whether the result is odd or even. Compute H(X) and H(Y) in bits. Explain why different entropies can describe the same underlying physical experiment.







NoteSuggested solution





For the exact result X, each of the eight faces has probability 1/8, so

H(X)=-8\left(\frac18\log_2\frac18\right)=3\text{ bits}.

For parity Y, odd and even each have probability 1/2, so

H(Y)=-2\left(\frac12\log_2\frac12\right)=1\text{ bit}.

The physical experiment is unchanged, but X and Y represent different descriptions of its outcome. Knowing the exact face answers a more detailed question than knowing parity. In this case parity is a deterministic coarsening of the exact result and necessarily discards information about which face occurred.




4. A confident but poor forecast. A binary process has generating success probability 0.70. Compare predictions q(1)=0.70, q(1)=0.50, and q(1)=0.99. Compute their expected log losses and rank them. Which predictive model has the smallest entropy? Does this answer the same question as ranking by expected log loss?







NoteSuggested solution





For a generating success probability p(1)=0.70 and prediction q(1)=r, expected log loss is

H(p,q)=-0.70\log r-0.30\log(1-r).









Predicted r
Expected log loss (nats)
Entropy of the model (nats)




0.70
0.611
0.611


0.50
0.693
0.693


0.99
1.389
0.056



Thus the expected-loss ranking, from best to worst, is 0.70, 0.50, 0.99. The 0.99 model has the smallest entropy, since it is most certain of its prediction, but it has the worst expected loss. Its occasional failures are extremely costly under log loss. Entropy measures uncertainty within q; cross-entropy measures q’s expected predictive performance under p.




5. Derive the KL identity. Starting from the definitions of entropy and cross-entropy, show that D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=H(p,q)-H(p). Explain what remains fixed when we compare two candidate predictions q_1 and q_2 against the same p.







NoteSuggested solution





By definition,

H(p)=-\sum_xp(x)\log p(x),\qquad
H(p,q)=-\sum_xp(x)\log q(x).

Subtracting,

\begin{aligned}
H(p,q)-H(p)
&=-\sum_xp(x)\log q(x)+\sum_xp(x)\log p(x)\\
&=\sum_xp(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\\
&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q).
\end{aligned}

When comparing q_1 with q_2, the generating distribution p and the evaluation target remain fixed. In particular, H(p) is a constant common to both comparisons. Therefore,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_1)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_2)
=H(p,q_1)-H(p,q_2).

This is why differences in expected predictive log loss can rank the models even though H(p) is generally unknown. The calculation assumes common outcomes and finite values where needed; if q(x)=0 for an outcome having p(x)>0, the corresponding divergence is infinite.




6. Direction matters. Using Bernoulli distributions with p(1)=0.8 and q(1)=0.5, calculate both D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q) and D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p). Explain their differing interpretations without calling either quantity a geometric distance.







NoteSuggested solution





For p(1)=0.8, q(1)=0.5, and complementary probabilities p(0)=0.2, q(0)=0.5,

\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
&=0.8\log\frac{0.8}{0.5}+0.2\log\frac{0.2}{0.5}\\
&\approx0.193\text{ nats},\\[5pt]
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)
&=0.5\log\frac{0.5}{0.8}+0.5\log\frac{0.5}{0.2}\\
&\approx0.223\text{ nats}.
\end{aligned}

The first is the extra expected loss from using q to predict observations generated by p. The second reverses those roles: q generates observations and p provides predictions. The expectations weight the two outcomes differently, so there is no reason for the values to match. Neither is an ordinary geometric distance.




7. Model comparison without knowing p. You receive 100 new outcomes and predictive probabilities from two models that were fit without using those outcomes. Write Python code to compute their mean held-out log losses. Explain why the difference in observed mean log loss can be useful even though you do not know the entropy of the generating distribution.







NoteSuggested solution





With binary outcomes y_i\in\{0,1\} and predictions q_i=P(Y_i=1), compute

\widehat L=-\frac{1}{100}\sum_{i=1}^{100}
\left[y_i\log q_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-q_i)\right].

Here is executable example code. In a real analysis, replace the simulated outcomes and the two example forecast arrays with the 100 held-out observations and their corresponding model predictions.

rng_solution_7 = np.random.default_rng(107)
outcomes = rng_solution_7.binomial(1, 0.7, size=100)
model_1_probs = np.full(100, 0.65)
model_2_probs = np.full(100, 0.85)

def heldout_log_loss(y, prob_success):
    y = np.asarray(y)
    prob_success = np.asarray(prob_success)
    assert y.shape == prob_success.shape
    assert np.all((prob_success > 0) & (prob_success < 1))
    return float(-np.mean(
        y * np.log(prob_success)
        + (1 - y) * np.log1p(-prob_success)
    ))

loss_1 = heldout_log_loss(outcomes, model_1_probs)
loss_2 = heldout_log_loss(outcomes, model_2_probs)
print(f"Model 1: {loss_1:.3f} nats/observation")
print(f"Model 2: {loss_2:.3f} nats/observation")
print(f"Model 2 minus Model 1: {loss_2 - loss_1:+.3f}")

Model 1: 0.598 nats/observation
Model 2: 0.631 nats/observation
Model 2 minus Model 1: +0.033


A positive value of loss_2 - loss_1 favors Model 1 on these observations; a negative value favors Model 2. For a fixed generating distribution, the theoretical difference is

H(p,q_2)-H(p,q_1)
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_2)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_1),

because H(p) cancels. The observed difference estimates this comparison without knowing H(p). With only 100 observations, however, sampling variation remains; a small difference is not conclusive. Probabilities must correspond to the same held-out observations, and models must not have been fit on these observations.




8. Simulated overfitting. Extend the grouped Bernoulli experiment in Section 5. Run at least 100 independent repetitions and report the mean training and held-out log loss for the pooled and separate-groups models. Repeat with 6, 30, and 100 training observations per group. Describe what changes and why. (Avoid selecting only runs that support your preferred conclusion.)







NoteSuggested solution





We repeat the same experiment using 12 groups, a common generating probability of 0.70, and 300 independent test observations per group. Both models use the same (k+1)/(n+2) smoothing rule as in Section 5. This code executes 200 independent repetitions for each training sample size and averages all results, not just selected runs.

rng_solution_8 = np.random.default_rng(108)

def simulation_scores(train_per_group, n_repetitions=200,
                      n_groups=12, test_per_group=300,
                      true_probability=0.70):
    values = np.empty((n_repetitions, 4))

    for rep in range(n_repetitions):
        train = rng_solution_8.binomial(
            1, true_probability, size=(n_groups, train_per_group)
        )
        test = rng_solution_8.binomial(
            1, true_probability, size=(n_groups, test_per_group)
        )

        pooled = (train.sum() + 1) / (train.size + 2)
        by_group = (train.sum(axis=1) + 1) / (train_per_group + 2)

        q_pooled_train = np.full(train.shape, pooled)
        q_pooled_test = np.full(test.shape, pooled)
        q_group_train = np.broadcast_to(by_group[:, None], train.shape)
        q_group_test = np.broadcast_to(by_group[:, None], test.shape)

        values[rep] = [
            mean_log_loss(train, q_pooled_train),
            mean_log_loss(test, q_pooled_test),
            mean_log_loss(train, q_group_train),
            mean_log_loss(test, q_group_test),
        ]
    return values.mean(axis=0)

print("n/group | pooled train | pooled test | group train | group test")
for n in (6, 30, 100):
    scores_mean = simulation_scores(n)
    print(f"{n:7d} | " + " | ".join(f"{s:12.4f}" for s in scores_mean))

n/group | pooled train | pooled test | group train | group test
      6 |       0.6028 |       0.6162 |       0.5353 |       0.6623
     30 |       0.6109 |       0.6127 |       0.5953 |       0.6268
    100 |       0.6098 |       0.6112 |       0.6053 |       0.6158


The separate-groups model generally achieves lower training loss, especially with six observations per group, because it can adapt to each group’s sampling noise. Yet in this experiment the true probability is identical across groups, so that added flexibility offers no real predictive advantage. Its held-out loss is generally higher for small training samples.
As the number of observations per group increases, the separate estimates become more stable and approach the common generating probability. The discrepancy in held-out performance narrows; any residual difference will vary across Monte Carlo repetitions. The pooled model uses more observations to estimate the same underlying probability and is generally more efficient under this particular generating assumption. This conclusion would not automatically carry over to genuinely heterogeneous groups or models with different pooling assumptions.
If preferred, use the two columns of held-out scores from each repetition to calculate standard errors or plot the distribution of paired differences; reporting only the mean does not show their variability.




9. Two scientific explanations. Construct two different plausible causal stories that produce the same probability distribution for the observations being evaluated. Explain why predictive log scores alone cannot choose between the stories.







NoteSuggested solution





Let X and Y be binary. Consider the following two causal stories:

Story A: X is generated as a fair Bernoulli variable. It then causes Y, which agrees with X with probability 0.8.
Story B: Y is generated as a fair Bernoulli variable. It then causes X, which agrees with Y with probability 0.8.

Both stories imply exactly the same observational joint distribution:




Y=0
Y=1




X=0
0.40
0.10


X=1
0.10
0.40



Thus every observed pair (X,Y) receives the same predictive probability and the same log score under either story. The causal interpretations differ, however. Under Story A, intervening to set X=1 would give P(Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X=1))=0.8; under Story B, intervening on X does not change the marginal distribution of its presumed cause Y, so P(Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X=1))=0.5.
The observational predictions alone cannot identify which direction of causation is correct. An intervention or some other defensible causal assumption would be needed to distinguish the stories.




10. Reflection. Consider the claim: “This model has a lower KL divergence, so it has learned more information about the world.” Identify which parts of the claim are justified, which are ambiguous, and what additional context would be required.







NoteSuggested solution





Justified, under specified conditions: If the intended comparison is D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_1)<D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_2), both models predict the same outcome under the same generating distribution p, and the divergences are well defined, then q_1 has lower expected predictive log loss than q_2.
Ambiguous: “More information” does not specify a particular quantity. KL divergence in this comparison measures the predictive discrepancy between distributions, not how much data the model observed, how much its posterior changed, or the practical importance of its predictions. Nor does a lower divergence prove that the model recovered the true mechanism.
Needed context: We must specify the direction of KL divergence, the common reference/generating distribution, the outcomes and measurement scale being scored, how the models produced their predictions, and whether the claimed difference is exact or estimated from data. If estimated, we should consider sampling uncertainty and the validity of the evaluation procedure. A different question—such as how much a posterior differs from a prior—would use a different KL comparison and require a different interpretation.
A more defensible conclusion is: “For the stated predictive target and generating distribution, this model has smaller expected excess log loss.”

We have two hypotheses:

A: The panda belongs to species A.
B: The panda belongs to species B.

The problem gives us the following information:




Species A

Prior probability

Probability of twins
0.10

Probability of singleton
0.90

We will use T for a twin birth, S for a single birth. We will also make explicit the assumption that the birth outcomes are independent conditional on the mother’s species (that is, once we know the mother’s species then there is no other information available that could be used to change the probability of the outcome of a future birth).
We know the mother has already given birth to twins. We want:

P(T_2\mid T_1)

where T_1 represents twins on the first birth and T_2 twins on the second.
Note that the first twin birth changes our beliefs about the mother’s species.
Before observing the first birth, we had:

P(A)=P(B)=0.5

After observing twins, we apply Bayes’ theorem:

P(A\mid T_1)
=\frac{P(T_1\mid A)P(A)}{P(T_1)}

The denominator is calculated using the law of total probability:

P(T_1)=P(T_1\mid A)P(A)+P(T_1\mid B)P(B)

Substituting:

P(T_1)=(0.1)(0.5)+(0.2)(0.5)=0.15

Therefore:

P(A\mid T_1)=\frac{0.1(0.5)}{0.15}=\frac13

Similarly:

P(B\mid T_1)=\frac23

We now have updated beliefs about the species. The second birth can be twins under either hypothesis, so:

P(T_2\mid T_1)
=P(T_2\mid A)P(A\mid T_1)+P(T_2\mid B)P(B\mid T_1)

Substituting:

=\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\left(\frac13\right)
+\left(\frac15\right)\left(\frac23\right)


P(T_2\mid T_1)=\frac16\approx16.67\%

The probability we calculated is greater than the original probability of 15%. Since observing twins makes species B more plausible, and species B has a higher twin-birth rate, we would expect some increase in our resulting probability.



2H2




Click to show answer

This is actually the intermediate calculated we performed in the earlier question.
Using our notation from part 1:
We want:

P(A\mid T)

Using Bayes’ theorem:

P(A\mid T)=
\frac{P(T\mid A)P(A)}
{P(T\mid A)P(A)+P(T\mid B)P(B)}


=\frac{(0.1)(0.5)}
{(0.1)(0.5)+(0.2)(0.5)}


P(A\mid T)=\frac13\approx33.33\%

We were originally given P(T|A) which is a description of how likely the observation of twins is under our hypothesis that the panda is species A. What we just calculated is how plausible our hypothesis of species A is given that we have observed the event that twins were born.



2H3




Click to show answer

Now we have a second birth, this time a single.
We now want:

P(A\mid T_1,S_2)

From the second part, our updated probabilities are:

P(A\mid T_1)=\frac13,\qquad P(B\mid T_1)=\frac23

We can treat these as the priors for our next update.

P(A\mid T_1,S_2)=
\frac{P(S_2\mid A)P(A\mid T_1)}
{P(S_2\mid A)P(A\mid T_1)+P(S_2\mid B)P(B\mid T_1)}

Substituting:

=\frac{0.9(\frac13)}
{0.9(\frac13)+0.8(\frac23)}


=\frac{0.3}{0.3+0.53333}


P(A\mid T_1,S_2)=0.36

This problem is a useful demonstration of sequential Bayesian inference. Note that the evidence does not necessarily push us consistently toward one hypothesis, we now consider species A to be slightly more plausible.

We now have a new observation: the genetic test reports species A.
The test has:

Note that the second probability is the false-positive rate: a species B panda has a 35% chance of being identified as species A.

Part 1
Using equal prior probabilities:

P(A\mid +)=
\frac{P(+\mid A)P(A)}
{P(+\mid A)P(A)+P(+\mid B)P(B)}


=\frac{(0.8)(0.5)}
{(0.8)(0.5)+(0.35)(0.5)}

The positive genetic test favors species A, but because the test is imperfect, we do not have an extreme-valued probability.


Part 2
We already calculated:

P(A\mid T_1,S_2)=0.36


P(B\mid T_1,S_2)=0.64

We can use these as our new priors when incorporating the test:

P(A\mid T_1,S_2,+)
=\frac{P(+\mid A)P(A\mid T_1,S_2)}
{P(+\mid A)P(A\mid T_1,S_2)+P(+\mid B)P(B\mid T_1,S_2)}

Substituting:

=\frac{(0.8)(0.36)}
{(0.8)(0.36)+(0.35)(0.64)}


=\frac{0.288}{0.288+0.224}


P(A\mid T_1,S_2,+)=0.5625

title: Chapter 3
text:
Chapter 3 is focused on sampling as vehicle for using the posterior distribution to make inferences about the parameters of a model. The posterior distribution is a probability distribution that represents our beliefs about the parameters of a model after observing data. Remember that we generate the posterior by combining the prior distribution and the likelihood of the observed data.
As stated in the book, working with samples allows us to both side-step the need for integral calculus (assuming we can calculate an analytical solution at all) and that much of the modern methods used for computing the posterior distribution only produce samples themselves.

title: Chapter 3
text:
Easy
A Python version of the code in the text is:

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import binom

# Construct a grid of 1000 possible values for p
p_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)

# Uniform prior
prior = np.ones(1000)

# Binomial likelihood: 6 successes in 9 trials
likelihood = binom.pmf(6, n=9, p=p_grid)

# Calculate and normalize the posterior
posterior = likelihood * prior
posterior = posterior / posterior.sum()

# Draw 10,000 samples from the posterior
rng = np.random.default_rng(100)

samples = rng.choice(
    p_grid,
    size=10_000,
    replace=True,
    p=posterior
)



With two helper functions to make calculating the questions involving intervals easier:

def percentile_interval(samples, probability):
    """
    Return an equal-tailed posterior interval
    containing the specified probability.
    """
    tail = (1 - probability) / 2

    return tuple(
        np.quantile(samples, [tail, 1 - tail])
    )


def hdi(samples, probability):
    """
    Return the narrowest interval containing
    at least the specified fraction of samples.

    This is a sample-based approximation of
    the highest density interval (HDI).
    """
    ordered = np.sort(np.asarray(samples))

    n = len(ordered)
    k = int(np.ceil(probability * n))

    # All candidate intervals containing k samples
    lower = ordered[:n - k + 1]
    upper = ordered[k - 1:]

    # Find the narrowest
    widths = upper - lower
    i = np.argmin(widths)

    return (lower[i], upper[i])



An overview of the functions / methods we can use is:









Operation
Purpose






np.mean(...)
Calculate the proportion of samples satisfying a condition




np.quantile(samples, q)
Find a posterior quantile




hdi(samples, 0.50)
Find the narrowest 50% interval




percentile_interval(samples, 0.50)
Find the equal-tailed 50% interval

title: 17: Conditional Probability Revisted
text:
Recall that for two events A and B, with P(A)>0, the conditional probability of A given B is
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
Learning that B has occurred can change the set of possible outcomes under consideration.
We now extend this idea from events to random variables.

title: 17: Conditional Probability Revisted
text:
Conditional Expectation
Recall that the expectation of a discrete random variable is:

E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x)

If we know that Y=y, we use the conditional distribution:
E[X\mid Y=y]=\sum_x x\,p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)
Equivalently using the definition of conditional probability, we can write this as:

E[X\mid Y=y]
=
\frac{\sum_x x\,p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}

Note that now since we can condition on another random variable, we do not necessairly have a number as the result of the expectation. Instead, we can have a random variable as the result of the expectation.

E[X] is a number representing the unconditional mean of X.
E[X\mid Y=y] is a number representing the mean of X when Y is fixed at a particular value y.
E[X\mid Y] is itself a random variable, obtained by evaluating the conditional mean at the observed value of Y.

For example, if g(y)=E[X\mid Y=y], then E[X\mid Y]=g(Y).


Consider the joint PMF

\begin{aligned}
P(X=1,Y=1)&=0.5\\
P(X=1,Y=2)&=0.1\\
P(X=2,Y=1)&=0.1\\
P(X=2,Y=2)&=0.3
\end{aligned}

We want to calculate E[X\mid Y=1].


It is often easier to view the joint PMF as a table:




Y=1
Y=2
p_X(x)




X=1
0.5
0.1
0.6


X=2
0.1
0.3
0.4


p_Y(y)
0.6
0.4
1.0





We now need to determine the conditional distribution. We know that Y is restricted to 1, so we need only to concern ourselves with the first column of our table.

P(Y=1)=0.5+0.1=0.6.

We then have,

P(X=1\mid Y=1)=\frac{0.5}{0.6}=\frac56

and

P(X=2\mid Y=1)=\frac{0.1}{0.6}=\frac16.

Now we can calculate the conditional expectation:

\begin{aligned}
E[X\mid Y=1]
&=1\cdot P(X=1\mid Y=1)\quad+2\cdot P(X=2\mid Y=1)\\
&=1\cdot\frac56+2\cdot\frac16.
\end{aligned}

Thus,

E[X\mid Y=1]=\frac{7}{6}



Assuming the same joint PMF from the above example, what if we instead condition on Y=2?
Similarly as to before, we obtain:

P(X=1\mid Y=2)=\frac{0.1}{0.4}=\frac14

and

P(X=2\mid Y=2)=\frac{0.3}{0.4}=\frac34.

Therefore,

E[X\mid Y=2]
=1\cdot\frac14+2\cdot\frac34
=\frac74.


After this, we now have the complete conditional expectation function

g(y)=
\begin{cases}
\frac{7}{6},&y=1,\\
\frac{7}{4},&y=2.
\end{cases}

And so, E[X\mid Y] is a random variable that takes these two values according to the value of Y.
Note that averaging the conditional expectations according to the probabilities of Y gives

\begin{aligned}
E[g(Y)]
&=\frac76(0.6)+\frac74(0.4)\\
&=1.4\\
&=E[X].
\end{aligned}

First, you should verifiy that E[X] = 1.4.
Seeing this, we have that averaging the conditional expectations over all the probabilities of Y gives us the expectation of X itself. This is an instance of the law of total expectation, which we will cover as a general principle further on.

title: 17: Conditional Probability Revisted
text:
Obtaining Distributions by Conditioning
Conditioning can transform one probability distribution into another.

Suppose X_1\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_1,p) and X_2\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_2,p) with X_1 and X_2 independent.
We want to determine P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=m).
 
We first apply our definition of conditional probability:

P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=m)
=
\frac{P(X_1=k,X_1+X_2=m)}
{P(X_1+X_2=m)}.

We can then do some rearrangment from X_1=k,\quad X_1+X_2=m to X_1=k,\quad X_2=m-k. We then have:

P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=m)
=
\frac{P(X_1=k,X_2=m-k)}
{P(X_1+X_2=m)}.



We will now rewrite the numerator. Because we know that X_1 and X_2 are independent we have that:

P(X_1=k,X_2=m-k)
=P(X_1=k)P(X_2=m-k).

Then using their binomial PMFs,

P(X_1=k)
=\binom{n_1}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n_1-k}

and

P(X_2=m-k)
=\binom{n_2}{m-k}p^{m-k}(1-p)^{n_2-m+k}.

Our resulting numerator is then:

P(X_1=k,X_2=m-k)
=
\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{m-k}
p^m(1-p)^{n_1+n_2-m}.



Now we rewrite the denominator. We will use a useful property of independent binomial random variables where if they have the same success probability then their sum is also a binomial random variable that has the form:

X_1+X_2\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_1+n_2,p).

Our demoninator is then:

P(X_1+X_2=m)
=
\binom{n_1+n_2}{m}
p^m(1-p)^{n_1+n_2-m}.



After our rewrites, we now have:

\frac{
\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{m-k}
p^m(1-p)^{n_1+n_2-m}
}{
\binom{n_1+n_2}{m}
p^m(1-p)^{n_1+n_2-m}
}.

Note that the probability terms cancel, giving us

P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=m)
=
\frac{\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{m-k}}
{\binom{n_1+n_2}{m}}

for

\max(0,m-n_2)\leq k\leq\min(n_1,m).

This is the hypergeometric distribution.

The process of conditioning in this example converted our problem into a fundamentally different one than what is represented by the binomial distribution.
Before conditioning, the number of successes in each group is binomial. But after conditioning on the total number of successes, the problem becomes one of allocating a fixed number of successes across two groups. This is the same as the sampling-without-replacement problem represented by the hypergeometric distribution.
Where if have n_1 red balls and n_2 green balls. If we select m balls uniformly without replacement, the probability of selecting exactly k red balls is

P(X=k)
=
\frac{\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{m-k}}
{\binom{n_1+n_2}{m}}.

Something important in the above expression is that the resulting conditional distribution does not depend on p. This happens because knowing the total number of successes eliminates the information contributed by the common success probability, leaving only the combinatorial allocation of those successes.


Suppose that X_1\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_1) and X_2\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_2) where the random variables are independent and \lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.
We will determine the conditional PMF of X_1 given X_1+X_2=n.
First, we will write the conditional probability. For k=0,1,\ldots,n

P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=n)
=
\frac{P(X_1=k,X_2=n-k)}
{P(X_1+X_2=n)}.



Next, we will evaluate the numerator.
Using independence and the Poisson PMF,

\begin{aligned}
P(X_1=k,X_2=n-k)
&=
\frac{e^{-\lambda_1}\lambda_1^k}{k!}
\frac{e^{-\lambda_2}\lambda_2^{n-k}}{(n-k)!}\\
&=
\frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)}
\lambda_1^k\lambda_2^{n-k}}
{k!(n-k)!}.
\end{aligned}



Finally, we will evaluate the denominator.
Using the property that the sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson, with parameter equal to the sum of the individual parameters, we have:

X_1+X_2\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)

and

P(X_1+X_2=n)
=
\frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)}
(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^n}{n!}.

Substituting and canceling gives us:

\begin{aligned}
&P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=n)\\[2mm]
&\quad=
\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}
\frac{\lambda_1^k\lambda_2^{n-k}}
{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^n}.
\end{aligned}

Recognizing the binomial coefficient lets us rewrite the above as:

P(X_1=k\mid X_1+X_2=n)
=
\binom nk
\left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}\right)^k
\left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}\right)^{n-k}

This is a binomial PMF with success probability

q=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}.

Therefore,

X_1\mid(X_1+X_2=n)
\sim
\operatorname{Binomial}
\left(n,\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}\right)


Considering our above example, imagine two independent sources generating events.
Source 1 produces events at an average rate \lambda_1 while source 2 produces events at an average rate \lambda_2.
Without additional information, the event counts from the two sources are independent Poisson random variables.
If we observe exactly n events in total, then conditioned on this information, each observed event can be attributed to source 1 with probability

\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}.

Thus the number attributable to source 1 is binomially distributed.
This is useful in applications involving arrivals, queueing systems, reliability, and event-count models.


Consider an experiment with three possible outcomes where each trial produces outcome 1, 2, or 3, with respective probabilities p_1,\qquad p_2,\qquad p_3, where p_1+p_2+p_3=1.
Suppose n independent trials are performed and let X_i denote the number of trials producing outcome i.
We will to determine E[X_1\mid X_2=m].


First, we note that the random vector (X_1,X_2,X_3) follows a multinomial distribution:

(X_1,X_2,X_3)
\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n;p_1,p_2,p_3).

Where X_1+X_2+X_3=n.


Now, knowing that X_2=m tells us that exactly m of the trials produced outcome 2. Then, the remaining n-m trials must have produced outcome 1 or outcome 3. Understanding this, we know that we now need to renormalize the probabilities of these remaining outcomes.
In a trial that does not produce outcome 2, the probability of outcome 1 is

P(\text{outcome 1}\mid\text{not outcome 2})
=
\frac{p_1}{1-p_2}.

Since 1-p_2=p_1+p_3 we have

P(\text{outcome 1}\mid\text{not outcome 2})
=
\frac{p_1}{p_1+p_3}.



Among the n-m remaining trials, each produces outcome 1 with the conditional probability we just found above.
Therefore,

X_1\mid X_2=m
\sim
\operatorname{Binomial}
\left(n-m,\frac{p_1}{1-p_2}\right).

This holds for p_2<1 whenever the conditioning event has positive probability.
We can now finally compute the expectation. The expected value of a binomial random variable with parameters r and q is rq and so the expectation is:

E[X_1\mid X_2=m]
=
(n-m)\frac{p_1}{1-p_2}
=
(n-m)\frac{p_1}{p_1+p_3}


Note that the expected count is not simply (n-m)p_1.
This is because the original probability p_1 describes the chance of outcome 1 before any restrictions are imposed. Once we know that a trial was not outcome 2, the relevant probability becomes

\frac{p_1}{1-p_2}.

Conditioning changes the entire distribution, not only the number of trials.

title: 12: Joint Distributions
text: Jointly distributed random variables are for the scenarios where we are working with multiple random variables simultaneously rather than just one in isolation. For simplicity, we will generally use two random variables in the definitions and examples below.

title: 12: Joint Distributions
text:
The Linearity of Expectation
The expectation of a sum is always equal to the sum of the expectations:: E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}X_{i}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}E[X_{i}]

We will show the linearity of the expectation:
E[\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}X_{i}]=

Note that this property holds true whether the random variables are independent or not.

What is the expected value of the sum obtained when 10 fair dice are rolled?


Trying to find the probability distribution for the sum of 10 dice (which ranges from 10 to 60) is very complicated. Instead, we define the total sum X as the addition of 10 individual random variables: X = X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_{10}
Here, X_i represents the outcome of the i-th die roll.
Recall that the expected value of a single die roll is 3.5.
Applying the linearity of expectation, we can sum the individual expectations: E[X] = E[X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_{10}] = E[X_1] + E[X_2] + \dots + E[X_{10}]
E[X] = 10 \times 3.5 = 35
And so the expected sum is 35.


At a party, N men throw their hats into the center of a room. The hats are mixed up, each man randomly selects one. What is the expected number of men who select their own hat?


Trying to calculate the exact probability of 0, 1, 2, or N men getting their hats requires complex combinatorics (derangements).
Instead, we use an idea called an Indicator Random Variable. Indicators (sometimes called dummy variables) are a special type of variable that takes on 1 if some condition is met and 0 otherwise.
Let I_i be an indicator for the i-th man:

I_i = 1 if man i gets his own hat.
I_i = 0 if man i does not.

The total number of men who get their own hat (X) is the sum of these indicators:
X = I_1 + I_2 + \dots + I_N
To find the expected value of an indicator variable, we only need to find the probability of the event occurring.
Since the hats are assumed to be random (that is, uniformly and arbitrarily selected), the chance that man i grabs his specific hat out of the pile of N hats is 1/N.
Therefore, E[I_i] = \frac{1}{N}.
Now we apply linearity of expectation.
Despite that the variables are not independent (if man 1 grabs man 2’s hat, man 2’s probability is affected), the linearity of expectation is not affected by this.
E[X] = E[I_1] + E[I_2] + \dots + E[I_N]
E[X] = \frac{1}{N} + \frac{1}{N} + \dots + \frac{1}{N} \quad \text{(summed } N \text{ times)}
E[X] = N \left( \frac{1}{N} \right) = 1
The expected number of men who get their own hat is 1. Note that this holds regardless of whether there are 5 men or 5,000 men at the party.

title: 12: Joint Distributions
text:
Discrete Variables
Let X and Y be discrete random variables with a joint Probability Mass Function (PMF) given by the following table:




Y=1
Y=2
Y=3




X=0
0.1
0.2
0.1


X=1
0.3
0.1
0.2





To find the marginal distribution of X, denoted P(X=x), sum the probabilities across all possible values of Y (summing across the rows):
P(X=x) = \sum_{y} P(X=x, Y=y)
P(X=0) = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.1 = \mathbf{0.4}
P(X=1) = 0.3 + 0.1 + 0.2 = \mathbf{0.6}


To find the marginal distribution of Y, denoted P(Y=y), sum the probabilities across all possible values of X (summing down the columns):
P(Y=y) = \sum_{x} P(X=x, Y=y)
P(Y=1) = 0.1 + 0.3 = \mathbf{0.4}
P(Y=2) = 0.2 + 0.1 = \mathbf{0.3}
P(Y=3) = 0.1 + 0.2 = \mathbf{0.3}


Note that both marginal distributions sum to 1.0, confirming they are valid probability distributions.

title: 12: Joint Distributions
text:
Continuous Variables
Let X and Y be continuous random variables with the following joint Probability Density Function (PDF):
f(x,y) = x + y \quad \text{for } 0 \le x \le 1 \text{ and } 0 \le y \le 1

To find the marginal PDF of X, denoted f_X(x), integrate the joint PDF over all possible values of Y. Since the function is only defined from 0 to 1 for Y:
f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dy
f_X(x) = \int_{0}^{1} (x + y) \, dy
Evaluate the integral with respect to y, treating x as a constant:
f_X(x) = \left[ xy + \frac{y^2}{2} \right]_{y=0}^{y=1}
f_X(x) = \left( x(1) + \frac{1^2}{2} \right) - (0 + 0)
f_X(x) = x + \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{for } 0 \le x \le 1

To find the marginal PDF of Y, denoted f_Y(y), perform the exact same process, but integrate over all possible values of X:f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx
f_Y(y) = \int_{0}^{1} (x + y) \, dx
f_Y(y) = \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} + xy \right]_{x=0}^{x=1}
f_Y(y) = y + \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{for } 0 \le y \le 1

title: 8: Discrete Random Variables
text:
A discrete random variable is a rule that assigns distinct, separated numerical values to the outcomes of a random process.
Its set of possible values is countable. Formally, this is a mapping between the values and the set of natural numbers. Informally, this means you can list the values out, either finitely (like \{1, 2, 3\}) or infinitely (like the non-negative integers \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}).

title: 8: Discrete Random Variables
text:
Bernoulli
The Bernoulli random variable models a single trial with exactly two outcomes (commonly denoted as success/failure).
The probability of success (1) is p, and the probability of failure (0) is 1-p, where p \in (0,1).
Note that this interval is open, if we included the endpoints then we are allowing for the situation where the random variable would entirely predictable and so not random at all.

title: 8: Discrete Random Variables
text:
Binomial
The Binomial random variable extends the Bernoulli concept to n independent trials, calculating the probability of getting exactly i successes.
The PMF is given by:
p(i)=\binom{n}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i} \;\; \text{for} \;\; i=0,1,\dots,n

An airplane works if at least half of its engines work. Assume that we can model the engine failing probability as 1-p.
When is a 4-engine airplane safer than a 2-engine airplane?


Since the probability of an engine failing is 1-p, the probability of an engine functioning successfully must then be 1 - (1-p) = p.
We can model the number of working engines using the Binomial distribution.


For a 2-engine airplane to fly, at least 1 engine (half of 2) must work.
We sum the probabilities of exactly 1 and exactly 2 engines working (as these are mutually exclusive outcomes):
P(\text{2-engine success}) = \binom{2}{1}p^{1}(1-p)^{1} + \binom{2}{2}p^{2}(1-p)^{0}
P(\text{2-engine success}) = 2p(1-p) + p^{2} = 2p - p^{2}


For a 4-engine airplane to fly, at least 2 engines (half of 4) must work.
We sum the probabilities of exactly 2, 3, and 4 engines working:
P(\text{4-engine success}) = \binom{4}{2}p^{2}(1-p)^{2} + \binom{4}{3}p^{3}(1-p)^{1} + \binom{4}{4}p^{4}(1-p)^{0}
P(\text{4-engine success}) = 6p^{2}(1 - 2p + p^{2}) + 4p^{3}(1-p) + p^{4}
P(\text{4-engine success}) = 6p^{2} - 12p^{3} + 6p^{4} + 4p^{3} - 4p^{4} + p^{4} = 3p^{4} - 8p^{3} + 6p^{2}


To find when the 4-engine airplane is safer, we set its success probability greater than or equal to the 2-engine airplane’s success probability:
3p^{4} - 8p^{3} + 6p^{2} \ge 2p - p^{2}
3p^{4} - 8p^{3} + 7p^{2} - 2p \ge 0
Factoring out p gives:
p(3p^{3} - 8p^{2} + 7p - 2) \ge 0
This factors to:
p(p-1)^{2}(3p-2) \ge 0
Because p is a probability between 0 and 1, p is positive and (p-1)^{2} is always positive. We can then divide by these terms without concern about division by zero or reversing the inequality.
Therefore, the inequality holds true only when:
3p - 2 \ge 0
p \ge 2/3


So, a 4-engine airplane is safer than a 2-engine airplane only when the probability of a single engine working successfully is at least 2/3.

The Poisson distribution is used to model the number of events occurring during an interval.

The average number of particles appearing in one second is 3.2. What’s the probability that no more than 2 such particles appear in one second?


We can solve this by defining a Poisson random variable X representing the number of particles appearing in one second.
We are given the average rate \lambda = 3.2. And we need to find the probability that no more than 2 particles appear, which is P(X \le 2).
Appealing to the compement rule we can sum the probabilities of exactly 0, 1, and 2 particles appearing:
P(X \le 2) = P(X=0) + P(X=1) + P(X=2)
Using the Poisson PMF formula P(X=i)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^{i}}{i!}:
P(X=0) = e^{-3.2}\frac{3.2^0}{0!} = e^{-3.2}(1) = e^{-3.2}
P(X=1) = e^{-3.2}\frac{3.2^1}{1!} = 3.2e^{-3.2}
P(X=2) = e^{-3.2}\frac{3.2^2}{2!} = e^{-3.2}\frac{10.24}{2} = 5.12e^{-3.2}
Now, we sum these probabilities together:
P(X \le 2) = e^{-3.2} + 3.2e^{-3.2} + 5.12e^{-3.2}
P(X \le 2) = e^{-3.2}(1 + 3.2 + 5.12)
P(X \le 2) = 9.32e^{-3.2}
After calculating this, we get approximately 0.3799, meaning there is about a 38% chance that 2 or fewer particles will appear in that one-second window.

Application to the 3-Category Digit Problem
Suppose you want to know how many n-digit strings contain:

Exactly a zeros
Exactly b odd digits
Exactly c even non-zero digits

where a + b + c = n.
Using the multinomial structure:
Assign the locations: \binom{n}{a, b, c} = \frac{n!}{a!b!c!} ways to decide which positions hold which category.
Fill each category:

a spots filled with \{0\}: 1^a ways.
b spots filled with odd digits: 5^b ways.
c spots filled with even non-zero digits: 4^c ways.

The total count is:
\binom{n}{a, b, c} 1^a 5^b 4^c = \frac{n!}{a!b!c!} 5^b 4^c
Summing this over all non-negative integers where a + b + c = n reconstructs the entire space:
\sum_{a+b+c=n} \binom{n}{a, b, c} 1^a 5^b 4^c = (1 + 5 + 4)^n = 10^n
Just as the Binomial Theorem tracks taking a left or right turn at each step, the Multinomial Theorem tracks navigating an m-way intersection at every step of length n.

We have already discussed the idea of conditional probability during our introduction to sample and state spaces. But this was in the context of the general idea of probability itself. We will now focus on how the incorporation of new information is computed.
What should happen to a probability when we learn something new?
Suppose we draw one card from a standard 52-card deck.
Before seeing the card:
P(\text{Ace})=\frac{4}{52}=\frac{1}{13}.
Now suppose someone tells us:
Does that information matter?
Yes.
We now know that the card must be one of the 13 Hearts.
Among those 13 cards, only one is an Ace.
Therefore,
P(\text{Ace}\mid\text{Heart})
=
\frac{1}{13}.
In this particular example the probability happened not to change.
Now changing the information:
There are 12 Face Cards, and 3 of them are Hearts.
If we ask for the probability that the card is a Heart:
P(\text{Heart}\mid\text{Face})
=
\frac{3}{12}
=
\frac14.
Our new information changed the probability from
P(\text{Heart})=\frac{13}{52}=\frac14
to
P(\text{Heart}\mid\text{Face})=\frac14.
But again, this new information did not change it.
We will now choose something that does.
Now:
P(\text{Heart}\mid\text{Spade})=0.
The new information makes Hearts impossible.
Conditional probability fundamentally asks:
The word among is extremely important.

title: 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Interpretation 1: Restricted sample space
Knowing B occurred restricts our sample space from \Omega to B.
Then we ask how much of B is also in A.

title: 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Interpretation 2: “Among”
P(A\mid B) means:

Among the B cases, what fraction are also A?

For example:

Among students who own a laptop, what fraction are engineering majors?

The denominator is laptop owners, not all students.

title: 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Interpretation 3: Renormalization
The original probabilities of all outcomes outside B become zero. The probabilities inside B are rescaled so that they add to one.
This is particularly useful later when discussing Bayesian inference.


Roll a fair six-sided die.
Let
A=\{\text{even}\}
and
B=\{\text{greater than 3}\}.
The original sample space is
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.
The condition B tells us:
B=\{4,5,6\}.
So our universe is now:
\{4,5,6\}.
Of those three outcomes, two are even:
\{4,6\}.
Therefore,
P(A\mid B)=\frac{2}{3}.

What happened to 1, 2, and 3?
These outcomes became impossible given the information.

title: 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Independence and Mutual Exclusivity
Mutually exclusive:

Knowing one occurred tells you the other did not occur.

Independent:

Knowing one occurred tells you nothing about whether the other occurred.

These are almost opposite ideas.
For nonzero-probability events, mutually exclusive events cannot be independent.

Consider a single die.
Let
A=\{\text{roll a 1}\}
and
B=\{\text{roll a 6}\}.
These events are mutually exclusive. That is, they cannot happen simultaneously.
Therefore:
P(A\cap B)=0.
But:
P(B)=\frac16
while
P(B\mid A)=0.
Knowing that A occurred changes the probability of B. Therefore they are not independent.

Along a path: multiply

P(B)
=

title: 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Formulating Bayes’ Theorem
Start with the multiplication rule:
P(A\cap B)
=
P(A\mid B)P(B).
But we can also write the same intersection in the opposite direction:
P(A\cap B)
=
P(B\mid A)P(A).
Since both expressions equal the same quantity,
P(A\mid B)P(B)
=
P(B\mid A)P(A).
Therefore,
\boxed{
P(A\mid B)
=
\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}
}
Bayes’ theorem is not an unrelated new formula but instead a consequence of conditional probability. Fundamentally, Bayesian inference is built out of conditional probability.
